activities.anchor: feel only gentle warmth on their face
activities.caption: bet the arc's temperature
activities.name: wldArcEst

config.prompt: A welding arc burns at roughly what temperature?
config.why: About 6,000 °C — as hot as the sun's surface — and the damage arrives as ultraviolet radiation the body cannot sense in real time: an unprotected glance of a second or two inflames the eye's surface hours later.
config.context: roughly 6,000 °C — sun-on-earth, with no heat warning attached

activities.anchor: injuries that announce themselves too late
activities.caption: match each hazard to its delay
activities.name: wldDelayMatch

config.prompt: The gap between cause and consequence — match hazard to delay:

pairs.right: burns the eye hours after the glance
starts an hour after the last spark
arrives with no warning at all

config.why: Welding safety is largely the craft of defending against injuries that arrive on their own schedule — which is why the trade answers them with systems, not reflexes.

activities.caption: the hierarchy of controls, top to bottom
activities.name: wldHierOrder

config.prompt: Defences ranked by how little they depend on someone remembering to comply:
items: Eliminate or engineer the hazard away — remove combustibles, fit local exhaust ventilation, put up welding screens
Administrative controls — permits, fire watches, daily equipment inspections
Personal protective equipment — helmet, gloves, leathers, respirator: the last line, not the first
config.why: A helmet protects one wearer during one arc; a ventilation system protects everyone in the building, every day, for years — including the day someone forgets their gear.

activities.anchor: at ten metres an arc can still burn retinas and skin
activities.caption: place the everyday filter plate
activities.name: wldShadePlace

config.prompt: Everyday-amperage stick and MIG call for a filter plate in a band — place the middle of that band:
config.why: Stick and MIG at everyday amperages call for shades around 10–13; oxyacetylene's gentler radiation uses around 4–6 — and bystanders matter as much as welders, which is why screens go up around the work.

activities.anchor: born when the arc vaporises metal
activities.caption: match the metal to what its fume carries
activities.name: wldFumeMatch

config.prompt: Fume chemistry follows the work — match metal to hazard:

pairs.right: iron and manganese — a neurotoxin under chronic exposure
zinc oxide — metal fume fever, a flu-like illness arriving hours after the shift
whatever was on the surface, vaporised with the metal

config.why: Welding fume is not smoke — it is a fine aerosol of metal oxides and silicates, condensed into particles small enough to reach deep into the lungs, accumulating dose across thousands of arcs.

activities.anchor: thins fume rather than removing it
activities.caption: one line of this fume plan is wrong
activities.name: wldFumeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this shop's fume plan is wrong — click it:
lines: Local exhaust ventilation: extraction nozzle within about 30 cm of the arc, capturing the plume at source.
Capture works by proximity — an arm parked half a metre away can run noisily and still capture almost nothing.
General dilution with fans and open doors is the first choice — moving air everywhere beats capture at one point.
Respirators with fume-rated filters back up what capture cannot reach.
Exposure limits are set in milligrams per cubic metre over an eight-hour shift.
config.correction: General dilution is the weaker second choice — it only dilutes the hazard; capture at the source takes it out of the air entirely, which is why the extraction arm sits within 30 cm of the arc.
config.why: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies welding fume overall as a carcinogen — the reason even mild-steel fume is treated seriously.

activities.anchor: The defences are procedural and cheap
activities.caption: damp gloves and a scuffed lead — decide
activities.name: wldShockBranch

config.root: Morning rain left your gloves damp, and a lead's insulation looks scuffed. The job is due. Decide:

start.text: What do you do before striking an arc?

choices.label: Weld anyway — 60 volts is low voltage
choices.feedback: Open-circuit voltages of 60–100 volts are enough to drive dangerous current through damp skin — and shock happens when the body bridges the electrode side to the work.

choices.label: Swap to dry insulated gauntlets, inspect and replace the lead, check dry footing — then strike
choices.feedback: The whole defence list, and every item is cheap: dry gloves, daily lead inspection, a well-clamped work lead, dry footing, never standing in water.

choices.label: Just keep bare skin off the workpiece when changing rods
choices.feedback: That closes one bridging path — but the damp gloves and the scuffed insulation remain open ones.

risk.text: The circuit does not care about deadlines — tens to hundreds of amps at 60–100 volts open-circuit take the body as a conductor.

fix.text: Inspection and dry insulation — the system that makes shock a non-event.

partial.text: Procedural habits only work as a set — one remaining path is one too many.

config.why: A welding circuit runs tens to hundreds of amps; the body only has to bridge electrode side to work — wet gloves, damaged insulation, coiled cables and damp footing are all bridges.

activities.anchor: treat every cylinder as a rocket with a valve
activities.caption: true or false — cylinders and their chemistry
activities.name: wldGasJudge

statements.s: Oxygen is flammable, which is why it is stored apart from fuel gas.
statements.why: Oxygen is not flammable — it is the ingredient every fire needs; in concentrated form it makes ordinary materials burn violently.

statements.s: Oil or grease on an oxygen fitting can ignite spontaneously under pressure and flow.
statements.why: Oxygen equipment never touches hydrocarbons — and fuel-gas cylinders are stored apart from oxygen.

statements.s: Acetylene becomes unstable above roughly 15 psi, so its regulators are set low.
statements.why: And its cylinders are used upright — the gas is dissolved in acetone within a porous filler; tipped over, the solvent can leak out with the gas.

statements.s: A cylinder may be rolled on its side across the shop floor to save time.
statements.why: Cylinders ride proper carts, stand upright and chained — a falling cylinder can shear its own valve and turn 50 kilograms of steel into a projectile.

statements.s: Flashback arrestors stop a flame travelling back into the hose.
statements.why: Valves on the fuel-gas lines — plus regulators inspected for creeping gauges and hoses for cracks.
